title: Biinterpretability of computably enumerable degrees with arithmetic
formal: Does R admit a parameter-free first-order interpretation of standard arithmetic together with a parameter-free definable map assigning each degree an index of a c.e. set of that degree?
definitions: A set A of natural numbers is computably enumerable (c.e.) if a finite ordinary Turing program enumerates exactly A. Write A≤_T B when an oracle Turing machine with membership access to B decides membership in A on every input. Equivalence under mutual reducibility defines a Turing degree. R is the set of degrees containing a c.e. set, ordered by ≤_T; it is not the set of all degrees below the halting problem. All quantification over degrees below is over R. The language has only ≤ and logical equality, with no named degrees or parameters unless explicitly stated. Fix an effective standard numbering e↦W_e of c.e. sets. An interpretation means a finite k, a parameter-free definable domain U⊆R^k, a parameter-free definable equivalence relation E on U, and parameter-free definable relations on U invariant under E whose quotient is isomorphic to (N,0,1,+,×). Thus the interpreted model must be standard, not merely satisfy first-order arithmetic. A coding map is a parameter-free formula F(a,u) invariant under E such that each a∈R is associated with exactly one E-class, and if this class corresponds to e∈N in the arithmetic isomorphism, deg_T(W_e)=a. All formulas are finite first-order formulas in ≤ and equality. The interpretation and map are fixed once for the whole structure, not chosen separately for each a. No named degree parameters may be used.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation, with exactly the structures and quantifiers specified here. A positive answer must supply the interpretation and coding relation with their properties. A double-jump index or a parameter-dependent coding does not suffice.
context: The 1998 introduction formulates the degree-index version and distinguishes it from a weaker map separating double-jump classes. Parameter-free coding implies rigidity.
why: Full biinterpretability would recover individual computability degrees from order-theoretic information.

import_provenance.original_title: Biinterpretability of computably enumerable degrees with arithmetic
import_provenance.original_statement: Can standard arithmetic be interpreted inside the pure order of computably enumerable Turing degrees with a definable coding map assigning each degree an index for a c.e. set of that same degree? This would upgrade Nies–Shore–Slaman’s biinterpretability up to the double jump to full recovery of individual c.e. degrees.

context_blocks.text: The 1998 introduction formulates the degree-index version and distinguishes it from a weaker map separating double-jump classes. Parameter-free coding implies rigidity.

sentences: Standard arithmetic must be reconstructed inside the order of c.e. degrees.
Its numbers are definable equivalence classes of finite tuples of degrees.
A single definable map must attach an arithmetic index to every degree.
The indexed c.e. set must have that very degree.
Both the interpretation and the coding map must be parameter-free.
